source.title: The Pitfalls of Simplicity Bias in Neural Networks
source.authors: Harshay Shah; Kaustav Tamuly; Aditi Raghunathan; Prateek Jain; Praneeth Netrapalli

page_placements.theme: Simple and spurious features link memorization to subgroup and shift failures

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests feature reliance, randomized labels/noise, optimization choices and regularization on purpose-built synthetic and image-based datasets. Its results refine the broader simplicity-bias framing, but do not test the claim’s random-label memorization or training-time comparison.
record.gate_note: The paper directly reports one appendix experiment training on randomized labels, but does not report training error or test error for it. It reports randomized-feature accuracy/AUC results and performance on noisy-label datasets; these are not measurements of fitting completely random labels. The paper’s discussion of prior random-label work is cited background, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures simplicity bias and feature reliance, not any version's random-label fitting or learning dynamics. Random-label memorization is cited as background. Contrary to the record, supplied Appendix C.4 contains no randomized-label experiment or statement that randomizing labels leaves the outcome unchanged.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's main conclusion paraphrase is accurate: on the proposed synthetic and image-based datasets, SGD-trained networks can exhibit extreme simplicity bias, ignore complex predictive features, and suffer robustness and generalization failures. Ensembles and adversarial training do not fully resolve these failures. The authors do not establish any of V1–V6.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines simplicity bias using synthetic and constructed image datasets, randomized-feature metrics, and targeted interventions; it does not reproduce the cited random-label memorization experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that outcome depends on feature simplicity and predictive power, dataset, model architecture, optimizer and activation, initialization, regularization, and adversarial-training perturbation budget. These concern simplicity bias, not the claim versions’ random-label fitting outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature randomization at evaluation yields approximately 0.5 AUC when the simplest feature is randomized and approximately 1.0 when complex features are randomized (Section 4.2; Tables 4–9). These measure feature reliance, not fitting randomized labels or unstructured training inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks trained on the constructed datasets can rely exclusively on the simplest predictive feature.

fits_no_version.finding: On the noisy-feature dataset, Table 2 reports training accuracy 0.984–0.999 and test accuracy 0.940–0.949. Labels remain predictable from noiseless slab features; Appendix D.1's discussion of overfitting noise concerns the linear feature and supplies no temporal comparison of real versus random labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A simple noisy feature can induce near-perfect training fit but inferior generalization despite available fully predictive complex features.

record.problems: No result for the randomized-label condition is numerically reported, and the text does not state its training or test error. Most experiments use constructed datasets; the paper’s conclusions about broader settings are presented as conjectures. Several results are presented only in figures, and the text does not provide exact values for them.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows: the text’s randomized-label statement in Appendix C.4 reports no outcome value or explicit result about training/test error; cited prior work is excluded.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random training labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time comparisons between true and random labels and convergence across label-corruption fractions.
Zero training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across random-label corruption fractions.
Regularization's effect on random-label fitting and the effect of removing regularization on true-label generalization.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's unsupported Appendix C.4 randomized-label finding and related gate-note and rows-left-out statements. C.4 varies dropout and weight decay on structured LMS-7 data; its randomized AUCs concern input features at evaluation. No qualifying result rows or verdicts are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random labels to near-zero training error with test error at chance, without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time for random versus true labels and convergence speed as the fraction of corrupted labels grows.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Whether training error remains perfect and test error rises steadily across corruption fractions from none to all.
Whether weight decay, dropout or data augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and their removal’s effect on true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before random or noisy labels over the course of training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The introduction cites random-label fitting as background without examining it or advancing an argument about the claim versions.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure simplicity bias and feature reliance; none tests or uses V1–V6.

source_check.notes: Section 4.2, Figure 3(b), and Appendices C.1–C.2 support the stated approximate AUCs. These measure evaluation-time feature randomization, not training on randomized labels; Appendix C.4 studies dropout and weight decay.
